description: How the 1982 Falklands War transformed Thatcher's fortunes and the 1984-85 Miners' Strike ended.
content_html:
The Falklands War, 1982

On 2 April 1982, Argentine military forces under President General Leopoldo Galtieri invaded the Falkland Islands — a British Crown Colony in the South Atlantic with a population of approximately 1,800 people, mostly of British descent. The Argentine government had long claimed sovereignty over the islands (calling them the Malvinas). Galtieri calculated that Britain, with a Conservative government cutting defence spending, would not respond militarily to retake distant islands.

Galtieri miscalculated. Thatcher’s response was immediate and decisive: a naval task force of over 100 ships, including aircraft carriers HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible, set sail within days. After intense diplomatic efforts led by US Secretary of State Alexander Haig failed, the task force entered the Total Exclusion Zone around the Falklands on 30 April 1982. The Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was sunk on 2 May with the loss of 323 lives — the most controversial act of the conflict. British losses included HMS Sheffield (4 May) and HMS Coventry (25 May). Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982 after 74 days of fighting. Total British military deaths numbered 255; Argentine deaths were approximately 649.

Key Fact

Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982. A British task force retook them by 14 June 1982, 74 days later. 255 British military personnel and approximately 649 Argentine forces were killed. The victory dramatically transformed Thatcher’s political standing from poll-trailing leader to national hero.

Political Impact of the Falklands

Before the Falklands, Thatcher’s government was deeply unpopular: unemployment had passed 3 million and polls showed Labour ahead. The Falklands victory transformed the political landscape. A wave of patriotic sentiment — dubbed the Falklands factor — boosted Conservative support dramatically. In the June 1983 general election, Thatcher won a landslide majority of 144 seats. Labour, divided over left-wing policies and standing on a manifesto that included nuclear disarmament and withdrawal from the EEC, suffered its worst result since 1935.

The 1983 victory gave Thatcher a mandate to pursue her programme of economic reform more aggressively. Privatisation accelerated, the trade union movement faced new legal restrictions, and the government prepared for the confrontation with the miners that had long seemed inevitable.

Historians debate how decisive the Falklands victory was in explaining the 1983 Conservative landslide. Some argue the Falklands factor was primary: Thatcher’s resolute leadership restored faith in British military power and national pride after decades of perceived decline. Others note that Labour’s deeply unpopular manifesto (nicknamed the “longest suicide note in history” by its own MP Gerald Kaufman), the continuing split between Labour and the new Social Democratic Party (SDP), and Thatcher’s own economic recovery by 1983 (falling inflation, early signs of growth) were equally or more important. The consensus is that the Falklands revived Thatcher’s personal popularity, which then made existing Conservative advantages more decisive.

The Miners’ Strike, 1984–85

The Miners’ Strike of 1984–85 was the most bitter industrial dispute in Britain since the General Strike of 1926. The National Coal Board (NCB), headed by American-born Ian MacGregor, announced the closure of 20 pits and the loss of 20,000 jobs. Arthur Scargill, the NUM’s combative president, called a strike from 6 March 1984 without holding a national ballot of all members — a decision that proved fatally damaging to the union’s cause.

The government had prepared carefully. Coal stocks had been built up at power stations during 1983. The police mobilised in unprecedented numbers to facilitate the movement of coal and protect working miners. The most violent confrontations were at Orgreave coking plant in Yorkshire (June 1984), where mounted police charged lines of striking miners. The strike divided mining communities: some pits — particularly in Nottinghamshire, where miners formed the breakaway Union of Democratic Mineworkers — continued working throughout. Without a national ballot, Scargill struggled to maintain legal solidarity and faced court injunctions against picketing.

Key Fact

The Miners’ Strike (March 1984 – March 1985) was led by NUM president Arthur Scargill against NCB pit closure plans. The absence of a national ballot undermined the strike’s legal standing and cohesion. After a year, miners returned to work without an agreement. The defeat broke the NUM’s power and accelerated pit closures.

Several factors combined to defeat the miners. Government preparation was meticulous: large coal stockpiles meant power stations could keep running. Police coordination across forces was unprecedented — thousands of officers were deployed nationally to manage picketing. The absence of a national ballot meant that when courts ruled secondary picketing illegal, the NUM had no legal protection. The working miners of Nottinghamshire further divided the union. Financial pressure on families grew through the long autumn and winter of 1984–85; NUM funds were sequestrated (seized) by the courts, removing resources. Public sympathy, initially with the miners’ communities, was damaged by violence on picket lines. By March 1985, many miners were forced back simply by hunger and debt. The defeat broke the NUM’s political power and was followed by rapid pit closures — more than had originally been announced.
exam_tip_html: On a 10-mark ‘Compare Interpretations’ question about the Falklands War or the Miners’ Strike, focus on the reasons interpretations differ. Ask: was the interpretation written during the events or long after? Does it use government sources (which emphasised national defence and the rule of law) or community/union sources (which emphasised job losses and police violence)? Authors’ political positions and the evidence they draw on — not just what they argue — are the key to accessing the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Argentina’s invasion of the Falkland Islands (2 April 1982) was defeated by a British task force by 14 June 1982; the “Falklands factor” revived Thatcher’s popularity and contributed to her landslide victory in the June 1983 general election.
  • The Miners’ Strike (March 1984 – March 1985) was led by NUM president Arthur Scargill against planned pit closures; the absence of a national ballot, government preparation and police mobilisation meant miners returned to work defeated after a year, breaking the NUM’s power.
  • Both events were defining moments of the Thatcher era — the Falklands demonstrating her resolve in foreign policy, the miners’ strike demonstrating her determination to break union power in domestic policy.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the British response to Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands in 1982.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Thatcher dispatched a task force of over 100 ships including aircraft carriers to the South Atlantic within days of the invasion.
• After diplomatic efforts failed, British forces entered the Total Exclusion Zone and began combat operations to retake the islands.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• NUM president Arthur Scargill called the strike from 6 March 1984 without holding a national ballot of all members, which undermined its legal standing.
• The most violent clashes occurred at Orgreave coking plant in Yorkshire in June 1984, between police and striking miners.
• Miners in Nottinghamshire continued working and formed the breakaway Union of Democratic Mineworkers.
• After a year on strike, miners returned to work in March 1985 without having achieved their aims.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the failure of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. absence of a national ballot, government coal stockpiles, or division among miners) and develops the mechanism in detail — showing how the cause operated and what specific effects it had on the strike’s ability to succeed.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Falklands War victory for Margaret Thatcher's government.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (the “Falklands factor” reviving Conservative support, or the 1983 landslide election victory with a 144-seat majority) and develops a chain — how the consequence unfolded and what further effects it had on Thatcher’s ability to pursue her economic programme.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Miners' Strike of 1984-85 for British industrial relations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (defeat of the NUM broke the most powerful union in Britain, accelerated pit closures, devastated mining communities) AND over time (weakened the trade union movement broadly, confirmed the shift from manufacturing to service economy, left enduring divisions in coalfield communities). Weighs limits: some mining communities retained strong union culture.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the strike without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Falklands War was more important than the Miners' Strike in shaping Thatcher's Britain.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument comparing both events — Falklands (boosted popularity, enabled 1983 mandate, shaped foreign policy image) and Miners’ Strike (broke union power, transformed industrial relations, devastated communities, accelerated economic shift). Weighs which had longer-lasting significance with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for both events. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but comparison is thin or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account of one or both events without sustained comparison.
[16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: On which date did Argentina invade the Falkland Islands?
Who led the National Union of Mineworkers during the 1984-85 Miners' Strike?
The task force sent to recapture the Falklands accepted Argentine surrender on _____ June 1982, after 74 days of conflict.
The NUM president called the 1984 strike without holding a national _____ of all members, which damaged the union's legal position.
Match each event to its description:
right: Surge of patriotic support that boosted Thatcher's poll ratings after the 1982 war
Yorkshire coking plant where violent clashes between police and miners occurred in June 1984
Breakaway union formed by Nottinghamshire miners who continued working during the 1984-85 strike

glossary_terms.definition: Argentine military dictator who ordered the invasion of the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982, seeking to divert attention from Argentina's domestic difficulties.
The Royal Navy and Royal Marines force sent to the South Atlantic in April 1982 to retake the Falkland Islands from Argentine occupation.

The surge of patriotic support experienced in Britain following the Falklands War victory, credited with reviving support for the Conservative government and contributing to the 1983 election landslide.
A year-long strike by the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), led by Arthur Scargill, from March 1984 to March 1985, against the Coal Board's programme of pit closures.
President of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) from 1982, who led the 1984-85 Miners' Strike and refused to call a national ballot of members before striking.
